extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, IP stakeholders (industry, academia, counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO guidance and case-law update on analyzing patent-eligible subject matter under Section 101/Alice, including clarifications to the Office’s two-step framework (Steps 2A and 2B) and examples from Federal Circuit decisions. Includes indicators examiners and practitioners should consider when evaluating computer-implemented and other technology claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework (Step 2A and Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Office’s two-step inquiry: determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A) and, if so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination provide an inventive concept that amounts to 'significantly more' (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Step 2A to assess whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (judicial exception). If a judicial exception is present, use Step 2B to evaluate whether the claim's additional elements provide an inventive concept — considering elements both individually and in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarified Step 2A — improvements in computer-related technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in computer-related technology are not limited to the operation of a computer or network per se, but may also include allowing computer performance of a function not previously performable by a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indication of an improvement in computer-related technology may include: (1) a teaching in the specification about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology; and (2) claiming a particular solution to a problem as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarified Step 2B — consider elements in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider additional elements in combination, as well as individually, when determining whether a claim amounts to 'significantly more' (i.e., whether there is an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate additional claim elements only in isolation; assess whether an ordered combination of elements provides something more than the judicial exception itself. BASCOM reiterated this combined-elements approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching in the specification as evidence of technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification teaching about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology is an indication that the claim may be directed to a specific technological improvement rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit disclosure explaining how the invention enhances computer performance, solves a technological problem, or enables a computer to perform functions it could not previously perform; such teachings support eligibility under Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming a particular solution vs. claiming an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a particular solution to a problem (concrete steps/implementation) are more likely to be seen as directed to a patent-eligible invention than claims that only recite the abstract idea of a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and examine claims to describe concrete, specific implementations and technical solutions rather than high-level concepts or goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional combination/arrangement of generic components
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility may be found from generic computer components working together in an unconventional manner to solve a technological problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amdocs: the court found the claimed invention 'entails an unconventional technical solution (enhancing data in a distributed fashion) to a technological problem (massive record flows...)'. Use evidence of unconventional arrangements that produce a technical improvement to support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve graphical user interfaces (GUIs) may not be abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting systems and methods for improving the display and interaction of information via a GUI, where the improvement has no 'pre-electronic trading analog', can be found not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trading Tech: claims that recite more than merely 'setting, displaying, and selecting' data — i.e., that produce an improvement in GUI functionality — can be eligible. Emphasize the specific GUI improvement and its technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and computer-related improvements appropriately claimed are not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Software and other improvements in computer-related technology are not abstract when they are appropriately claimed as providing a technical improvement or solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims recite concrete improvements to computer-related technology (e.g., performance, new capabilities, technical problem solutions), frame and analyze them as technological improvements rather than as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of secondary considerations in Section 101 analysis (question presented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a court must consider secondary considerations evidence (e.g., copying, unmet need, commercial success and failure of others) in its Section 101 analysis has been posed to the Supreme Court (DataTreasury petition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that secondary considerations are being litigated as potentially relevant to eligibility; preserve and present such evidence where appropriate, but note that its role in §101 is not settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between §101 and other patentability doctrines (novelty/obviousness/enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether issues of novelty, obviousness, and enablement (typical §102/§103/§112 inquiries) play a role in the §101 analysis is a question raised in petitions (e.g., Trading Tech en banc petitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ongoing debate about how much other patentability considerations should affect the Section 101 inquiry; document record evidence relevant to these doctrines when helpful to the §101 evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether features disclosed but not claimed may affect eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A question before the Federal Circuit (Amdocs en banc petition) asks whether features disclosed in the specification but not claimed may confer patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claim drafting captures the inventive technical features; when relying on specification disclosures to show a technical solution, be mindful of the limits of relying on unclaimed features to establish claim eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-precedential/precedential decisions as guidance (use facts/details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit decisions — both precedential and non-precedential — provide examples of how claims were evaluated for eligibility and the factual bases relied upon (e.g., Enfish, Bascom, Amdocs, Trading Tech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the reasoning and factual findings in these decisions as guidance: identify factual parallels (e.g., technological problem solved, unconventional arrangement, specific improvements) rather than relying on broad labels like 'abstract idea' alone.
